## Proof

We claim the inequality

$$\|f\|_{L^{\frac{np}{n-p}}(\mathbb{R}^n)} \le c\,\|\nabla f\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)}, \qquad f\in C_0^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n),$$

holds precisely for

$$\boxed{1 \le p < n.}$$

We prove necessity and sufficiency.

---

### Necessity ($p<n$ is required, and $p\ge 1$)

**Scaling argument forcing $p<n$.** Suppose the inequality holds for some $p$ with constant $c$ independent of $f$. For $f\in C_0^\infty$ and $\lambda>0$, set $f_\lambda(x)=f(\lambda x)$. Then

$$\|f_\lambda\|_{L^q} = \lambda^{-n/q}\|f\|_{L^q}, \qquad \|\nabla f_\lambda\|_{L^p} = \lambda^{1-n/p}\|\nabla f\|_{L^p},$$

where $q=\frac{np}{n-p}$. The inequality applied to $f_\lambda$ gives

$$\lambda^{-n/q}\|f\|_{L^q} \le c\,\lambda^{1-n/p}\|\nabla f\|_{L^p}.$$

For this to be consistent with the inequality for $f$ itself for **all** $\lambda>0$, the powers of $\lambda$ must match:

$$-\frac{n}{q} = 1-\frac{n}{p} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \frac{1}{q}=\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{n} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; q=\frac{np}{n-p}.$$

This relation is meaningful (gives $q>0$ finite) **only when $p<n$**. If $p\ge n$, then $1/p-1/n\le 0$, so $q\le 0$ or is undefined — no positive exponent $q$ satisfies the scaling law, and the inequality cannot hold for any finite $q$. Hence $p<n$ is necessary.

**Why $p\ge 1$.** For $p<1$ the "norm" $\|\cdot\|_p^p$ is not subadditive (the triangle inequality fails), and the standard Sobolev construction below breaks down; the inequality as a norm inequality is not valid for $p<1$. Thus we need $p\ge 1$.

---

### Sufficiency ($1\le p<n$): the Gagliardo–Nirenberg–Sobolev inequality

We sketch the standard construction. The key estimate is the **one-dimensional Sobolev inequality**: for $\varphi\in C_0^\infty(\mathbb{R})$,

$$\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R})} \le \|\varphi'\|_{L^1(\mathbb{R})}, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad |\varphi(t)|\le\int_{-\infty}^{t}|\varphi'(s)|\,ds.$$

Applying this coordinatewise to $f\in C_0^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$, for each $i=1,\dots,n$,

$$|f(x)| \le \int_{-\infty}^{x_i}|\partial_i f(\dots)|\,ds_i \;\le\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\partial_i f|\,ds_i =: g_i(\widehat{x_i}),$$

where $\widehat{x_i}$ denotes all coordinates except $x_i$. Thus $|f(x)|\le g_1\cdots g_n$ pointwise after multiplying the $n$ coordinate bounds. Raising to the power $1/(n-1)$ and integrating iteratively (using Hölder with exponents $(n-1,\dots,n-1)$, which is admissible since $n\cdot\frac{1}{n-1}=\frac{n}{n-1}$), one obtains the **case $p=1$**:

$$\|f\|_{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathbb{R}^n)} \le \prod_{i=1}^n\|\partial_i f\|_{L^1}^{1/n} \le \|\nabla f\|_{L^1}.$$

This is the Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality at $p=1$, giving $q=\frac{n}{n-1}=\frac{n\cdot 1}{n-1}$.

**General $1<p<n$.** Apply the $p=1$ result not to $f$ but to $g=|f|^\gamma$ with $\gamma=\frac{p(n-1)}{n-p}>0$ (positive since $p<n$). Then $g\in C_0^\infty$ up to regularization, and

$$\|g\|_{L^{n/(n-1)}} \le \|\nabla g\|_{L^1}.$$

The left side is $\bigl(\int |f|^{\gamma n/(n-1)}\bigr)^{(n-1)/n}$, and $\gamma\frac{n}{n-1}=\frac{np}{n-p}=q$, so the left side equals $\|f\|_{L^q}^{(n-1)/n\cdot\gamma}=\|f\|_{L^q}^{\gamma(n-1)/n}$.

For the right side, $|\nabla g|=\gamma|f|^{\gamma-1}|\nabla f|$, so

$$\|\nabla g\|_{L^1}=\gamma\int |f|^{\gamma-1}|\nabla f| \le \gamma\,\|f\|_{L^q}^{\gamma-1}\|\nabla f\|_{L^p}$$

by Hölder with exponents $\frac{p}{p-1}$ and $p$, since $\frac{(\gamma-1)p}{p-1}=\frac{p(n-1)/(n-p)-1}{\;}\cdot\frac{p}{p-1}=q$ (one checks $(\gamma-1)\frac{p}{p-1}=\frac{np}{n-p}=q$). Combining,

$$\|f\|_{L^q}^{\gamma(n-1)/n} \le \gamma\,\|f\|_{L^q}^{\gamma-1}\|\nabla f\|_{L^p}.$$

The exponent balance gives $\gamma(n-1)/n-(\gamma-1)=\frac{n-p}{n}\cdot\frac{p(n-1)}{n-p}-\frac{p(n-1)}{n-p}+1=\dots=1$, so dividing yields

$$\|f\|_{L^q} \le c_{n,p}\,\|\nabla f\|_{L^p}, \qquad q=\frac{np}{n-p}.$$

This is the desired inequality with $c=c_{n,p}$, valid for all $f\in C_0^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and every $1\le p<n$.

---

### Conclusion

The exponent $q=\frac{np}{n-p}$ on the left is exactly the **Sobolev conjugate** $p^*$, well-defined and the inequality valid precisely when

$$\boxed{1\le p<n.}$$

For $p\ge n$ the scaling exponent $1/p-1/n\le 0$ is non-positive, so no finite $L^q$-norm of $f$ can be controlled by $\|\nabla f\|_{L^p}$, and the inequality fails.

### PROOF COMPLETE
